reading.body:
NTT's Ashburn VA7 data center publishes 36 MW of IT capacity, which is 2.2 percent of Virginia's 1,639.4 MW of disclosed data center capacity.

The facility is one of only 26 sites in Virginia that publish a megawatt figure, out of 332 mapped facilities in the state. That gap is the real finding. Any state-level total built from published numbers describes a small, self-selected slice of the fleet, and the 306 sites that stay silent could sit on either side of it. Ashburn VA7 ranks 14th among the 26 disclosing sites, so it is mid-sized within the group that reports, not within Virginia's data center footprint as a whole.

For AI specifically, the published capacity is a power figure, not a workload figure. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 36 MW corresponds to roughly 900 racks and roughly 1,100 to 1,400 accelerators depending on configuration. Those are conversions from a density assumption, not disclosures. The 125,000 square feet of technical space is the only other physical constraint given, and it bounds how much of that capacity can be densely packed.

What the data does not cover is decisive. Nothing here states whether the facility is reserved for AI workloads, what its grid connection or interconnection status is, or whether it has announced expansion. The suitability score of 68 is a weighted mean of published IT capacity and operator type, with announced expansion listed as missing, so it measures disclosure as much as it measures the building. The site sits five miles from Dulles in Ashburn, where most of Virginia's published capacity concentrates, but concentration of disclosed capacity is not the same as concentration of load.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
